conversation.content: Let's have a conversation about designing a distributed key-value store. I've spent a fair amount of time working on similar systems — I was on the DynamoDB team at AWS for a few years. I'm interested in hearing how you'd approach it and where our experiences overlap or diverge.

That's great context. I led the internal KV store at my company — we served about 2 million QPS across 400 nodes. Started as a Redis cluster and evolved into a custom system when Redis couldn't meet our consistency and multi-region requirements. So I've lived this problem. Let me start with my framing: the fundamental design tension is between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance, but in practice, the real tension is between operational simplicity and performance. What matters most for this system?

I love that reframing. At DynamoDB, we learned exactly the same thing. The CAP theorem is a theoretical framework, but the daily pain is operational. Let's target: eventual consistency as default with optional strong reads, multi-region active-active, and 5ms p99 for reads. How do you partition the data?

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes — the standard approach. At my company, we started with 256 virtual nodes per physical node. But we learned something interesting: the number of virtual nodes has a sweet spot. Too few and you get uneven distribution. Too many and the routing table becomes large — with 400 nodes and 256 vnodes each, that's 102,400 entries that every node needs to know about. We eventually settled on 64 vnodes per node. The distribution was 'good enough' and the metadata was much more manageable. What was your experience at DynamoDB?

Interesting — we actually moved away from consistent hashing entirely at DynamoDB. The paper we published in 2022 describes the shift. Consistent hashing makes rebalancing smooth but the routing complexity, as you noted, grows. We switched to a partition table managed by a control plane. Explicit assignment of partition ranges to nodes. When you need to rebalance, the control plane orchestrates it. Less elegant mathematically, but much more predictable operationally. Did you consider that approach?

We did discuss it, actually. The argument against, for us, was the control plane as a single point of failure. With consistent hashing, any node can independently determine where a key lives — the ring is a distributed data structure. With a centralized partition table, if the control plane is down, new nodes can't join and partitions can't move. How did you handle that at Dynamo? I'd assume multi-Paxos or Raft for the control plane itself?

Exactly — the control plane runs on Paxos with 5 replicas. But here's the key insight: the control plane being down doesn't affect the data path. Every storage node caches a copy of the partition table locally. The table only changes during rebalancing, which is infrequent. Even if the control plane is down for an hour, reads and writes continue normally. The control plane only matters for administrative operations. In practice, we had better availability than the consistent hashing approach because there was no gossip protocol chatter or disagreement between nodes about ring state.

That's a compelling argument. The gossip protocol disagreement was actually one of our biggest operational headaches. Two nodes would occasionally have different views of the ring, leading to misrouted requests. Usually resolved in seconds, but for a financial services workload, even a few seconds of misroutes was problematic. If I were designing from scratch today, I'd probably go with your approach — a control plane for metadata and a purely data-path-focused storage layer. Separating the control plane from the data plane is a pattern that keeps proving its value.
Exactly. Now let's talk about replication. You mentioned multi-region active-active. That's where it gets really hard. How did you handle conflicts at your company?

We used last-writer-wins with hybrid logical clocks. Each write gets a timestamp that's a combination of physical time and a logical counter. When replicas diverge, the highest timestamp wins. It's simple and works for most use cases. But we had one critical use case — a counter for account balances — where LWW was unacceptable because it discards concurrent updates. For that, we implemented CRDTs — specifically a PN-counter. Each region maintains its own increment and decrement counts, and the merge function sums them all. Convergent by construction, no conflicts possible. The downside is that CRDTs only work for specific data types — you can't CRDT a general JSON blob.

CRDTs are powerful but limited, exactly as you said. At DynamoDB, we took a different approach for the general case — we let the application resolve conflicts. On a conflicting read, we return all versions and let the app decide. Amazon's shopping cart used this famously. The tradeoff is that it pushes complexity to the application developer, who often just picks 'last writer wins' anyway. But for the 10% of use cases where it matters, application-level resolution is more correct. What's your take on that tradeoff?

I think it depends on your customer base. If your customers are sophisticated infrastructure teams, application-level resolution works — they understand the semantics and can implement correct merge logic. If your customers are product engineers who just want a database, returning conflicting versions is a footgun. They'll write buggy merge logic or just pick a random version. At my company, we had both types of customers. We defaulted to LWW, offered CRDTs for specific types, and had a 'raw' mode that returned conflicting versions for the teams that wanted full control. Three tiers of sophistication. The trick was making the default safe and the advanced modes opt-in.
Three tiers — that's pragmatic. I like it. Let's discuss the storage engine. What did you use under the hood?

We started with RocksDB — Facebook's fork of LevelDB. LSM-tree based, excellent write performance. But we hit two problems at scale. First, compaction storms: when multiple SSTables compact simultaneously, the node's read latency spikes because disk I/O is saturated. We mitigated this with rate-limited compaction — cap compaction I/O at 60% of disk bandwidth. Second, space amplification: during compaction, you temporarily need both the old and new SSTables on disk. With 90% disk utilization, compaction fails and the node gets stuck. We learned the hard way to never exceed 70% disk utilization. We also experimented with a B-tree engine (BoltDB) for read-heavy workloads — B-trees have better read performance but worse write performance. Eventually we offered both as pluggable backends.

The compaction problem is very real. At AWS, we solved it differently — we moved to a tiered compaction strategy instead of leveled, which batches more work together. Fewer but larger compactions. The tradeoff is higher space amplification but more predictable latency. Have you looked into that?

We evaluated tiered compaction. The space amplification was the concern — at our data volumes, going from 1.1x (leveled) to 2-3x (tiered) space amplification meant terabytes of additional SSD. But your point about predictable latency resonates. In financial services, our SLA was on p99 latency, not storage cost. Tiered compaction's worst case is better even if its average is worse. If I were optimizing for latency SLAs, I'd switch to tiered. If optimizing for storage cost, I'd stay leveled. It also depends on the write/read ratio — tiered is better for write-heavy, leveled is better for read-heavy. At 2M QPS, we were roughly 70/30 reads to writes, so leveled was the right call for us.
That's a really nuanced analysis. Let me ask you an organizational question. You had 400 nodes. How big was the team operating this?

6 engineers and 2 SREs at peak. We got it down to 4 engineers and 1 SRE through automation. The biggest time sink was capacity planning and node replacement — SSDs fail, nodes die. We built an auto-replacement system: health checks detect a failing node, the control plane (in our case, a modified consistent hashing system) marks it as draining, replicas take over, and a new node is provisioned and data is rebalanced automatically. That single automation project freed up about 40% of the SRE's time. The second biggest time sink was customer support — 'why is my key-value read slow?' Almost always the answer was: their value was 2MB and they were surprised it wasn't fast. We added hard size limits and monitoring dashboards that teams could self-serve.

Ha — the 2MB value problem is universal. At DynamoDB we enforce a 400KB item limit for exactly that reason. Let's talk about something I find endlessly interesting: how do you handle hot keys? One key gets 100x the traffic of any other key.

This was our biggest production incident. A single key — a feature flag used by every request in the critical path — caused a node to saturate its NIC. Our approach after that incident: first, detection — track per-key request rates at the proxy layer using a probabilistic counter (Count-Min Sketch). When a key exceeds a threshold, it's flagged as hot. Second, mitigation — hot keys are automatically replicated to multiple nodes. Instead of one node serving that key, 5 nodes have a copy. The proxy load-balances reads across the replicas. Writes go to all replicas. Third, prevention — our client SDK has a local cache option. For immutable or slowly-changing values, clients cache locally and refresh on a TTL. The feature flag use case would have been solved by a 30-second client cache. At your scale with DynamoDB, did you handle this similarly?

Very similar. DynamoDB has adaptive capacity — if a partition is hot, we automatically split it and spread the load. For read-heavy hot keys, we added DAX — a write-through cache layer. Your approach of client-side caching for slowly-changing values is something we eventually launched as DynamoDB Accelerator's client-side component. Great minds think alike. Let me ask you one more thing: if you could go back and change one architectural decision in your KV store, what would it be?

I'd separate the control plane from the data plane from day one — which is what you described with DynamoDB's partition table approach. We spent 18 months patching gossip protocol issues that a proper control plane would have avoided. The second thing: I'd invest in a wire protocol early. We used a custom binary protocol that was fast but made client SDK development in multiple languages painful. We should have used gRPC from the start — the performance is close enough and the polyglot support is free. The third thing: schema validation. We let users store arbitrary bytes, and debugging issues when someone accidentally stored a protobuf as JSON or vice versa was a nightmare. Some guardrails on data formats would have saved hundreds of hours of support tickets.

Every one of those resonates. The wire protocol choice is something almost every infrastructure team gets wrong initially because custom binary feels like the right optimization. Anything you'd want to discuss that we haven't covered?

One area I find fascinating and underinvested in: observability for distributed storage. Standard metrics (latency, throughput, error rate) aren't enough. You need to see data distribution across partitions, replication lag per partition, compaction health per node, and client request patterns. We built a tool that visualized our hash ring with partition sizes as a heat map — you could instantly see imbalances. I'd advocate for building this kind of deep observability from the start, not as an afterthought. At scale, the system that you can't see is the system that will surprise you at 3 AM.

Couldn't agree more. This has been one of the best conversations I've had in an interview setting. You clearly have deep, battle-tested experience with distributed storage. The nuanced understanding of tradeoffs — compaction strategies, conflict resolution tiers, hot key mitigation — shows someone who's not just designed these systems but operated them in production at scale. Really enjoyed this discussion. Thank you.

strengths: Deep production experience with distributed storage — every answer backed by real-world learnings
Exceptional nuance on tradeoffs — compaction strategies, conflict resolution approaches, partitioning schemes
Strong ability to engage in peer-level technical discussion — learned from interviewer's experience while sharing own insights
weaknesses: API design was not formalized — no discussion of the client API, request formats, or error handling
Security was not addressed — no mention of authentication, authorization, or encryption
Capacity estimation was anecdotal (2M QPS, 400 nodes) rather than derived from first principles
